analysis.one_liner: Provides steady federal funding so communities can fix water and sewer systems and lower bills.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee for the rest of the 117th Congress without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would send roughly $35 billion a year from the Treasury to states for clean water and drinking water projects, with no yearly vote needed. It would pay homeowners to repair septic tanks and contaminated wells, replace lead pipes, fix school drinking fountains, and help small and rural systems. It would restrict most of the money to publicly owned water systems and let towns use the funds to buy private water companies, and it would require a national study of water bills, shutoffs, and unequal treatment.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with unaffordable water bills, people on failing septic systems, families with lead pipes or lead in school water, rural homes with contaminated wells, and tribal and small-town water systems all gain. Water and sewer construction workers gain from a large, steady pipeline of projects covered by prevailing-wage rules and project labor agreements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households with high water bills and unsafe water

how_it_helps.text: Transfers $18.1 billion a year for clean water programs and $16.4 billion a year for drinking water programs to the EPA, including $15.7 billion and $15.2 billion a year for the state revolving loan funds, automatically each October without a new appropriation.

Creates a grant program paying homeowners to repair, replace, or upgrade septic tanks and drainage fields, and makes permanent and expands a rural household water well grant program to $348.5 million a year.

Raises the school drinking water grant program from $5 million to $1.05 billion a year to make school fountains, coolers, and bottle-filling stations lead free and to test lead levels, and funds grants to replace residential lead service lines.

Requires a national EPA study of water affordability, rate increases, shutoffs for unpaid bills, discriminatory practices by water providers, and the effects on children, elderly, disabled, and other vulnerable households, with a report and recommendations to Congress within a year.

Lets states use loan funds to buy privately owned water and sewer systems and bring them into public ownership, and generally restricts new drinking water funding to publicly owned systems, with an exception for small systems serving under 10,000 people.

Adds grants for water systems contaminated by PFAS chemicals and for household well owners to install filtration, and bars states from using loan funds for projects that mainly benefit new subdivisions.
Requires American-made materials in drinking water projects and preserves prevailing-wage rules while encouraging project labor agreements on funded construction.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through roughly $34.85 billion a year in mandatory spending that is no longer subject to annual appropriation votes. Privately owned water and sewer utilities also bear a cost: state loan funds could be used to purchase their systems into public ownership, and most new funding would flow only to public systems.

drawbacks.text: The roughly $34.85 billion in annual mandatory transfers bypasses the normal yearly appropriations process, which reduces congressional control over how the money is spent.

The bill restricts most drinking water funding to publicly owned, operated, and managed systems, which disadvantages small private and investor-owned systems that would otherwise be eligible for loans.
Requirements to use American-made materials and project labor agreements can raise project costs and narrow the pool of eligible contractors, slowing construction in states with thin supply chains.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The scale is large but the problem is large too: water and sewer systems across the country need repair, bills have risen faster than incomes, and lead and PFAS contamination directly harm health. The main honest objections are the mandatory autopilot funding, which removes annual oversight, and the choice to route nearly all money through public systems, which is a deliberate policy choice to favor public ownership rather than a cost-neutral design. On balance the bill is a straightforward public investment in household water safety and affordability.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced, and no committee ever took it up before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on March 23, 2021.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
That was the last action of any kind: the committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the floor, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 with the bill still in committee.
Five Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Privately owned water utilities are better off, since the bill's public-buyout and public-only funding provisions died with it, and federal taxpayers avoided the roughly $35 billion a year in automatic spending. Households facing shutoffs, lead pipes, or PFAS-contaminated wells are no better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private water utilities and federal taxpayers

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only non-Democratic sponsor.

against.name: Tom Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill; it remained referred to his committee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew five Democratic cosponsors and its independent sponsor, no Republican cosponsors, and no recorded floor vote or debate either way.

industries.industry: Privately owned water and sewer utilities
industries.note: The bill generally restricts drinking water funding to publicly owned systems and lets municipalities use loan funds to buy private water and sewer systems into public ownership. It died before any of that took effect.

Roughly $35 billion a year in steady infrastructure funding would flow to construction, with American-made material requirements and prevailing-wage and project labor agreement provisions steering work toward union-signatory domestic contractors. Households get repaired systems; the industry gets a locked-in revenue channel.
A new federal grant program would pay homeowners directly for repairing or upgrading septic tanks and drainage fields, an estimated 20% of U.S. homes rely on.
